title: The Phulkian states
hookLine: Patiala, Nabha and Jind, often counted apart from the twelve

lines: A HUNGRY BOY BEFORE GURU HAR RAI.
cards: A hungry boy is brought before Guru Har Rai. Sikh tradition tells it simply: an uncle brings two small brothers to the Guru, and one of them pats his own empty stomach.
The Guru looks at the child and blesses him: his house will grow, and it will feed many. The boy's name was Phul.
Generations later, the families who traced their line to him ruled three states south of the Sutlej: Patiala, Nabha and Jind.

teach.h: SOME LISTS COUNT THEM, SOME DON'T.
teach.b: Here's the puzzle. Some lists of the twelve misls include the Phulkian states; others set them apart. Both habits have reasons.

teach.h: SOUTH OF THE SUTLEJ, IN MALWA.
teach.b: The Phulkian chiefs held the Malwa country, south of the Sutlej: different neighbors, different dangers, different deals. Another is how they ruled.
A misl was a band of equals around a chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa.

teach.h: RULING FAMILIES, NOT BANDS OF EQUALS.
teach.b: The Phulkian houses grew more like ruling families, leadership passing down a line, the chief becoming a raja.
Patiala's founder, Ala Singh, is remembered for building a state, and for making terms with the powers around him at times when other bands were fighting them.

Sikh histories judge those terms in more than one way: some call them shrewd survival, some a step away from the Dal Khalsa. So why are they here at all? Because the story starts with the Guru's blessing.
The Phulkian families traced their rise to that hungry boy, and they built and supported gurdwaras across their lands.
They stood apart in politics and stayed inside the same faith, the same scripture, the same Guru's house.
A family can live in a different town and still sit at the same table on the big days.

how: Sikh histories tell the story of Phul and Guru Har Rai's blessing, and gurdwaras in the former Phulkian lands, such as those in Patiala, are part of Sikh life in the Malwa region today.

o: a Guru who blessed the hungry and the poor
the blessed boy the Phulkian houses came from
the founder of Patiala, who made terms

s: every list of the misls counts the Phulkian states among the twelve

the Phulkian families traced their rise to a blessing from Guru Har Rai

games.q: you're the uncle who has brought two small boys before Guru Har Rai. one of them pats his empty stomach. what does the Guru do?
o: sends him away to be fed elsewhere.
blesses him, and his house after him.
tells him to come back when he's older.
games.why: tradition says the Guru blessed the boy, Phul, and his house. the families of Patiala, Nabha and Jind traced their rise to that blessing.

practice: Bring to mind a group you belong to, a family, a team, a congregation, and find the person who stands a little to the side of it: the cousin who moved away, the coworker who eats lunch alone.
Don't fix anything; just hold them in mind and notice what still connects them to the rest. Waheguru on each breath out, if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Phul, the boy Guru Har Rai blessed, whose line the Phulkian states, Patiala, Nabha and Jind, traced their rule to. Counted with the misls by some, set apart by others. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: apart, yet related. Politics apart, faith shared. That's day eight hundred ninety-nine.
